utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. We will have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone, Mr. Khan and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the Defence appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, with co-counsel Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic attorney from Croatia, representing Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my co-counsel, Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic appearing for Mr. Hazim Delic along with my co-counsel, Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, I am John Ackerman and along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray I appear on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before we continue this morning, the trial Chamber is sorry to announce that we might not be able to take the motion scheduled for this morning because of other more pressing problems. Would you mind if we take Tuesday morning for the arguments? Can we have the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours, for postponing that argument. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Witness T, who is a protected witness. I believe the blinds will have to be closed. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly let him swear. WITNESS T (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I begin, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may start. Examined by MS. McHENRY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, good morning. Do you understand that the judges have granted your request that your name and your face not be made public as part of your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that you will be known as Mr. T?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking the court usher to show you on a piece of paper a name and I ask you to confirm that it is your actual name. Is that your actual name that is written on the paper, sir? You do not have to say your name, just please tell me if that is your name, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, were you interviewed previously by a representative from the office of the Prosecutor and you gave a statement that was recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before giving that statement were you advised of certain rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have been here in The Hague today, have you again been advised of those rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, although you may remember them, just so the record is clear, do you understand that I am going to give you those rights again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you understand that you have the right to be assisted by counsel of your choice or to have legal assistance assigned to you without payment if you do not have sufficient means to pay for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand that you have the right to remain silent and to be cautioned that any statement you make shall be recorded and may be used in evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you mean against him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Against him or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It should be against you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct that no promises or inducements of any kind have been made to you from anyone in the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are testifying here voluntarily to this Tribunal today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have not requested a lawyer in connection with your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how old are you at the present time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 28.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when approximately you left Konjic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No English translation is coming through to me. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry sir, let me repeat the question. Can you tell the court when approximately you left Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then move to another country and do you still live in that country today? Not today, but at the present time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I moved to another country and then I later moved from there to a third country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, how far did you go in school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed secondary school as a metal worker, a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in early 1992, were you living in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1992 when you joined any kind of Defence or military force or unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of the war I joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you stationed as a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was stationed on the frontline in relation to Serb held territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the Konjic TO that you joined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when it was that you joined the Konjic TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what month that would be, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left the TO and joined another group or unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I later joined the Croatian Defence Council as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council, is that also known as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you state approximately if you know when it was that you joined the HVO police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe in April or May -- no, I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time that you were sent to the Celebici camp to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was sent there because HVO soldiers were providing the guards for the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this, approximately, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after the capture of Donje Selo. I cannot again recall the exact month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who sent you to work at Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sent by a commander called Zeljko Brekalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the HVO military police at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first went to the camp was everyone who worked in the camp a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to HVO there were Muslims and Croats, but I think there were members of the TO as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for an overview, how long in all did you remain working in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remained about six or seven months, maybe a little longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what month or what months it would have been when you left the camp finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was perhaps in October or November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties in the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately upon my arrival, the investigations of prisoners were carried out by the Ministry of the Interior, so that I was mainly bringing prisoners in for questioning, wait for them to complete the interview, then take them back to their place of detention. Later on, I was on duty at the telephone and then I became a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time period that you were a driver, can you explain what your duties were as a driver, what kinds of things you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mostly drove the prisoners when they were released to their villages, mostly to Donje Selo, because most of them were going there. That was one of my most important duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive people who worked in the camp on any occasions? Was that sometimes part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some cases, some instances, but not very significant, to take someone to a cafe or to a party or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also ever involved in moving prisoners between the Celebici camp and any other prison camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. As far as I can remember I once took the wounded from the camp in the centre of town, when they were wounded I drove them to the hospital, and then I think I later transferred them after treatment to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to the camp in the centre of town, sir, would that be what is referred to as Musala camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were a driver, who was the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Mucic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sometimes drive Mr. Mucic to the camp or away from the camp or between camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three times, not so often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic have his own transportation that he usually used when he was going to or from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had his own car and he usually used it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to his car, did Mr. Mucic have any other means of transportation that he sometimes used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a motorbike. As far as I recall, that is all, a motorbike and a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, was there ever any interruption in your work at Celebici camp, or did you work there continuously from when you first got there to when you finally left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an interruption when all the Croatian soldiers abandoned Celebici and joined the other Croats on the frontlines. That was the only time that I left the camp, and this was for a day or two. After that I went back to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please just briefly explain why you decided to go back to Celebici and how you made the arrangements to go back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reasons for leaving Celebici were the rumours going around town that the Croatian fighters would be blamed for certain things that were happening there, and another reason was the formation of the Muslim police, though I am not quite sure. When I came back I asked the commander, Zdravko Mucic, whether I could come back and he said I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain why it is that you wanted to go back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went back because it was boring to be in the military police. They were doing nothing, just sitting around. It was boring. There was no special reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you went back to Celebici then after talking to the commander, Mr. Mucic, were you a member of the TO, the HVO, some sort of police unit? Exactly when, if you know, were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth I do not know who I belonged to. Probably some kind of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you worked in the camp, did you sleep in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other persons also sleep in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What building did you and the other people sleep in? What was it called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not exactly know what it was called. I have forgotten the number now. Anyway it was the building where the offices were, and where the kitchen was for the guards, the canteen, I do not know whether it had a special name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of this witness's protected status and lack of a long pointer, I do not feel it necessary to use this model but if at some point your Honours think it would be helpful we can shut the blinds and have him do it. Sir, what was the ethnic background of the prisoners in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were of Serb ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the prisoners were detained? Was it in one place, more than one place? Can you please tell us the places where the prisoners were detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were detained in three places, two hangars and a tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of prisoners were kept in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the tunnel there were mainly people from Bradina, from Brdjani, mainly people who were considered a bit more dangerous, people who they thought had participated in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of prisoners were kept in the hangars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People in the hangars were mainly prisoners from Donje Selo, some from the centre of the town, mainly elderly people. There were some young people, but not that many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand that you do not remember the numbers of the hangars -- the two hangars where the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that the prisoners were kept either in the tunnel or in two hangars and I am asking if the hangars had numbers and if they did, if you remember the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangars did have numbers. It was number 6 and number 9, and the tunnel was number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the two hangars were, if you can just -- for instance, where was the -- let me start off. Was one hangar larger than the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One hangar was close to the place where the guards slept. That one was smaller and there was the other one in the back, the one in the back was much bigger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, previously you indicated that there were prisoners from the hangars in the centre of town. What town do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you previously mentioned that Zdravko Mucic was the commander of the camp. Did Mr. Mucic also have any kind of nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His nickname was Pavo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic commander of the camp in the very beginning when you first got to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not the commander at the time, the Ministry of Internal Affairs was in charge of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when Mr. Mucic was in charge of the camp, do you know whether or not he was a member of the TO, the HVO or the Ministry of Interior or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was probably a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before he became commander, did Mr. Mucic sometimes come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a deputy whose name was Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed Mr. Delic as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was probably Zdravko Mucic. I am not certain, probably. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delic have any injuries at any time when he worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before he became a permanent member of the prison, his leg was injured and he used crutches to walk on. Since he lived close to the prison he sometimes came there, and later he became a permanent member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he became a permanent member, was he deputy commander; in other words, did he have some position before he became deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely whether he held a position earlier or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Delic using his crutches when he first had a permanent position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delic have any kind of deputy or assistant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later he had a deputy named Sejo Mustafic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Mustafic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He mainly performed duties of the deputy when Pavo was away or when Hazim was away, he carried out -- he was responsible for the guards. He looked after the prisoners and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic have an office in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic's office face the camp or face the road outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently was Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes he would spend an hour or two in a day, then he would leave, he would not come back for two days, and so he was rather absent, absent more than present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was in the camp, what did Mr. Mucic do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he was there, he visited the prisoners, he spoke to some of them, asked them if they needed anything, the usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic normally inspect the hangars or the tunnel where the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did carry out inspections. As I said, he sometimes spoke to them. How many times I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the times when you saw Mr. Mucic speak to the prisoners, would it be inside the hangar or the tunnel or outside the hangars or the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The times I saw, it was outside the hangar. Whether he went inside the hangar or not when I was away, maybe he did, maybe he did not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you did not personally see him make any kinds of inspections inside the hangars or the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely. Maybe he did, maybe he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Mucic was not in the camp, do you know where he was or what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly where he was. His parents were there, maybe he stayed with his parents. He had a flat in town, maybe he slept there sometimes, but exactly where he was, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On some occasions, did you drive Mr. Mucic to places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes. I once drove him to see Mr. Zejnil -- actually he drove, I am sorry, but it was mainly -- I really do not know exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For instance, you indicated before, I believe, that Mr. Mucic sometimes went to cafes -- I am sorry, you indicated that sometimes you drove persons to cafes. I am wondering whether or not as part of your duties sometimes you drove Mr. Mucic to cafes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did drive, but that was not part of our duties. We would simply go for a drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about fishing. Did you ever go with Mr. Mucic fishing or drive him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you just spoke about a Mr. Zejnil. First of all, do you know the full name of Mr. Zejnil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position, if any, at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I knew and as the stories went in town, he was the main person, he was within the Territorial Defence. He was the main person for Prozor and Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Zejnil in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it the case that you cannot remember exactly or that -- exactly how many times, or you cannot remember whether he ever saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether I saw him or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any fears for you or your family as a result of your testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not that is affecting your ability to remember things or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That does have some influence and I also have a fairly bad memory, because these things happened almost seven years ago -- five years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not at the time you first were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor and since you have been at The Hague, on those occasions did you remember if you saw Mr. Delalic in the camp at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you cross-examining your own witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I am asking certain questions to find out -- I do not want to make representations to the court, but I think I am certainly entitled in these circumstances, this is certainly a very unusual situation and I am entitled to find out the basis for the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Possibly declaring a hostile eyewitness or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not done that yet, and I do not know in this kind of Tribunal such formalistic things are necessary, but I think at the moment I am entitled to enquire whether or not he has very quickly forgotten a number of things and I would ask permission to go forward, obviously he will answer as he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I address you on this matter? My learned friend has asked twice about his recollection, he has answered twice. He has told that he has answered to the best of his ability. I submit that that closes this matter, this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: About a particular matter, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can proceed on other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, generally, is it the case that when you are testifying here right now you are forgetting things that you knew within the last few days as well as when the Office of the Prosecutor interviewed you at the end of April of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not believe the witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a new question, different from his remembering whether Mr. Delalic has been in the camp or not. This is quite different. That was why I limited the possibility of pursuing the earlier question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object that she is impeaching her own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: She is not doing that. She is asking him other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember now, I did see him on one occasion when there was an oath being declared and once when he came to the office and he spoke to Mr. Zdravko Mucic; definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember, sir, if that was the only -- if those were the only occasions that you saw Mr. Delalic in the camp, or are you saying that you just cannot remember if there were other occasions also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are returning to the earlier question which you had abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You are right, your Honour, but given that he has given a specific answer to this question, I think I just need to clarify this. I am just trying to clarify exactly -- he now remembers something and I am trying to clarify exactly what he remembers. I am not doing anything other than trying to clarify the record. I am not trying to impeach him. I am just trying to find out what exactly his memory is. Sir, can you just say whether or not --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness has just answered that question precisely, twice and the exact occasions when he saw. There is no basis for different questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I might briefly respond. First of all, in general I would ask whether or not there is a rule that one Defence counsel objects for each accused, and secondly, I would ask that I think it is impossible to say that this witness's answer about what he does and does not remember is clear from this answer. Again I am not trying to impeach him, I am just trying to find out if he is sure those are the only times he saw Mr. Delalic or he does not remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember whether or not those are the -- can you say whether or not those are the only times Mr. Delalic came to the camp or whether or not you just do not remember if there were other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember seeing him twice, he did come to the camp. Whether he came again when I was away maybe yes, maybe no, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the workings of the prison; in other words were there written instructions to the guard, was there a code of conduct or procedure, were there regularly scheduled meetings? Can you just discuss how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no particular instructions for guards as to how to treat the prisoners. There were no meetings regarding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic normally communicate directly with the guards, or did he communicate with his deputy commander normally? Can you just explain a little bit about how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He usually communicated with Hazim Delic. He probably sometimes asked the guards how things were going on in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you in particular receive your instructions, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got instructions from Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive instructions from Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you worked at the camp, sir, can you describe the conditions for the prisoners? I would first ask you to describe the physical conditions, for instance the sleeping facilities, the toilet and bathing facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were very difficult, especially in the tunnel. People usually slept on concrete or on clothing they had, perhaps some extra clothing they had. As for hygiene conditions, they had some kind of improvised toilets. They sometimes took baths.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe how exactly it was that the prisoners took baths and approximately how frequently these occasions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends. Sometimes they washed once a week, sometimes they had one in three weeks, but it was mainly an improvised bath with cold water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just please explain a little bit more -- when you say it was improvised baths, exactly how did it work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They helped one another during the washing because, as I said, they did not have any special toilets or places to take baths, it was just cold water. They had a tap with holes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners would take a bath at the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember how many washed at the same time, but during the day, they would all finish the washing and they would be left out in the sun to dry so they could go back inside the hangar where it was much cooler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they wash themselves or did someone spray them with water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They washed each other, they helped each other wash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you yourself see this occasion where the prisoners were allowed to help each other wash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, was it just two or three prisoners there at a time or 200 prisoners there at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a group of five or six prisoners who were helping each other wash. When they finished there would be another group and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of this time period where the prisoners were allowed to wash each other and then sit outside in the sun to dry, do you know approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was some time in summer when it was very hot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if it was before or after the Red Cross visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was after the Red Cross visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequently did you yourself go inside the hangars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that often. The only thing was I would go to the door, I would go in from the door, but there was a very unpleasant smell inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the food the prisoners got, where it came from, what it was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They received food from the town, but exactly where they cooked it, I really do not know. It was some kind of soups, thick soups with bread. They received certain quantities of bread and sometimes they received sometimes twice a day, sometimes once a day, sometimes up to three times a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was that the prisoners received food three times a day and how frequent it was that the prisoners were fed three times a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when it was that they received food three times a day, but they mainly received food twice a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, going back for a minute, you indicated that there was a very unpleasant smell inside the hangar. Can you please explain why there was a very unpleasant smell inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was very hot and the hangar was built of aluminium and probably because people sweated inside and because they could not wash every day. That is probably why there was an unpleasant smell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prisoners and the guards eat the same food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the food for the guards come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very often food was prepared in the prison itself, and sometimes it was brought from town for the guards as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When food was prepared in the prison itself was that for the guards only, or was it also for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only for the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the food came from the town for the guards, was it the same food as the prisoners got or different food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only for the guards, it was different food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did any of the prisoners -- did the prisoners appear adequately nourished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. What do you mean "adequately"? I do not understand what the word "adequately" means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the prisoners appear like they had sufficient, enough food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have enough food and since food was not of very good quality, as I said, those were mainly soups, creamy soups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were there any manholes in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were, very close to the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any prisoners ever placed inside these manholes, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe exactly what you saw and heard about prisoners being placed in the manholes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mainly putting prisoners from the tunnel in there, as far as I know. I think that one of them was the brother of Zarko Mr.kajic, but I am not certain. They would leave them there, sometimes overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there was water in these manholes when the prisoners were placed in them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the prisoners were placed in the manhole, is this when you were a driver or before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was a driver, and whether they had done it before or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of toilet facilities were there in the tunnel, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same as in the hangars, they had improvised toilets somewhere on the side, but conditions were the same basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the court whether or not any of the prisoners were ever mistreated by being beaten or tortured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this just a few prisoners or was it more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a considerable number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it persons who worked in the camp or persons from outside the camp or both who beat the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done by some people from the camp and there were also people coming from the outside, outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know that prisoners were being beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes I saw it myself, such as in the case of Bato Kuljanin, when some team came from outside the prison and they took him inside to an office, and they beat him there for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what you saw or heard of this specific beating? Can you please tell us everything you remember about that, including when it was, how you knew about it, what you yourself could see or hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, when the policemen were killed in Repovci, they thought some Serbs had done it, and when the guards came back from Repovci they beat up the prisoners in the hangar in the back, and there were some other cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to some of the beatings that you yourself saw, did you know the name of the victim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, Zara Mrkajic, who was beat up once by some people coming from outside, I think they were from the MUP, I am not sure. Then his brother, I cannot recall his first name, then -- I mentioned Bato Kuljanin already. Then there was somebody called Mici, I cannot exactly remember his name. There were others but I cannot recall their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Bato Kuljanin, could you please tell us in more detail whether or not you remember anything about that beating in particular. For instance, do you remember when it was? When could you see and what could you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that the main reason was that they wanted to put the blame on him, that he had killed a soldier in Donje Selo during the operations there and the name of that soldier was Velija and they wanted to put the blame for that killing on him. By beating him, they wanted to force him to confess. As far as I heard later, he would not confess, and they beat him almost all night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you hear the beatings as they were going on? Could you hear anything when the beatings were going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one could hear his screams and moans and then he said that they had put scissors up his nose, they beat him with fists probably. When he came out I saw him. When he came out of the office, his whole head was black and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us exactly what you saw with respect to Zara Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion he was tied to a pillar, the electricity pile, the handcuffs. He was beaten before that and later he was tied to the pole and he was left there for about four or five hours. Then they beat him while he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who beat Zara Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were some people from outside the prison, not from the prison. I cannot say exactly, I cannot remember who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Zara Mrkajic's brother, please tell us exactly what you remember about that beating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the tunnel and he was reported to be a prominent Serbian soldier, so he received a lot of beatings. For a time he went on a hunger strike, he refused to eat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if he refused to eat or that he was not physically able to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he refused to eat. He went on a hunger strike, and then later, two or three days later, as far as I can recall, he started taking food again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated he received a lot of beatings. Can you estimate about how many times he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know I saw and heard that he was beaten at least three or four times. Whether it was more than that, I do not know, and who beat him, I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how about approximately when it was he was beaten. Even if you cannot remember the day, can you tell us what your duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mici, sir. Would you please tell the court what you yourself saw or heard with respect to the beating of Mici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that he was exposed to a lot of beatings in the prison, and I heard Zijad Landzo once boasting that he had beat him. All in all, I remember that he was beaten a lot because before the war they said that he was also a prominent Serb fighter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself ever see when Mici was beaten, or did you see his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw his injuries, but I did not personally observe the beating. I heard from Zijad Landzo that he had beaten him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have mentioned an Zijad Landzo. Can you please describe -- first of all, was Mr. Zijad Landzo a person inside the camp or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in the camp. He was a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he called Esad or did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a nickname, it was Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he called in the camp? Was he called by his nickname or by his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called him by his nickname, Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this person from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know his real name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt it in the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you see Zenga in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there non-stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else called Zenga in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else with the last name of Landzo in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo -- as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what Zenga looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not very tall, he was of medium height. He liked to have his head shaved. That is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, perhaps 18, 19, 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that you sometimes heard Zenga's voice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a very specific kind of voice, as if he spoke through the nose, nasally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you remember about him saying about the beatings of Mici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard him say on one occasion that he had beaten him up. For how long he beat him I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything about why he beat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything about how badly he had beaten him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what Zenga's attitude was when he talked about this? What was his demeanour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that. I think that calls for some kind of a conclusion about what this witness thinks his demeanour might have been. I do not think that is capable of description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think he said he boasted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry your Honour, if that is already in the record, I missed it. Sir, even if you yourself do not remember the name of the victim, did you also yourself see other beatings other than the ones where you have told us you remember the name of the victim? Do you need me to repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no need. It is difficult to remember the names of prisoners because these were people I saw for the first time, and there were many prisoners and all this happened five years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir, maybe my question was not clear. Is it the case that you yourself saw other beatings but you just now do not remember the name of the victim, or you never knew the name of the victim. In other words, I am not asking you the name of the victim, I am asking you whether or not other than the beatings you described of Bato, Zara, Zara's brother and Mici, did you yourself see other beatings even if you do not know the name of the victim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were some of these beatings that you saw done by persons who worked inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court what you yourself saw, and would you please start with a particular incident. Even if you do not remember the name of the victim, can you say what you yourself saw. If you know the names of the persons, the people who were doing the beating, what happened, can you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some guards for instance who came from other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebenica, Zepca who were there, as they were chased away by the Serbs from their towns and they were rather cruel with the prisoners, and some of them did not stay for long. Some of them did stay for longer periods, I cannot remember their names. They also beat the prisoners rather badly. For instance, on one occasion I saw Hazim hitting a prisoner with a crutch. I do not know the name. This was before he became deputy commander of the camp. On several occasions, he would use a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us the details, if you remember, of any -- the details of when you saw Mr. Hazim use a baseball bat to beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply when he saw a prisoner, he would, with no cause, take the bat, sometimes he would be carrying it on him, and he would hit him, without any reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Mr. Hazim, can you give us the last name of the Mr. Hazim you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any other persons in the camp use a baseball bat to beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zenga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you yourself saw Zenga do with the baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did not see him actually hitting people with a baseball bat, I heard this from other guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing Zenga with the baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever yourself see Zenga beat any prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him on one occasion when he set light to prisoners and this was recorded on the video. I cannot remember other occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides what you have already testified about Mici, were there ever any other occasions when you heard Zenga refer to his treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from other Serb prisoners with whom I was quite close.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I do not think he should be testifying about what he heard from other prisoners. That is hearsay; there is no name of those other prisoners; no establishment of any kind of reliability of what they might have said. The question was specific as to what he heard from Zenga or what he saw himself. It needs to be made clear that that is what he is being asked and his answers need to be specifically to that question, not what he heard from other people whose names we cannot even get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly limit your question to what he himself saw and heard directly from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to this question, I will, your Honour and then I may ask some other questions which can be resolved at that time. Sir, besides what you have already testified to about Mici, do you remember ever hearing anything from Zenga himself regarding his treatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would often say that they needed to be beaten. He simply enjoyed it. He would probably do the same to Croats if they had been there or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it also the case that on some occasions you heard from prisoners about their treatment from Zenga? I am now not asking you what they told you, I am just asking you if there were some occasions when prisoners told you about their mistreatment by Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that gets to the same place in a different direction. If he is permitted to testify that prisoners told him, whether he says what it was they said or not, the evidence is that they were telling him things that Zenga was doing. We have not got the names of any of those prisoners, there is no way to establish the reliability of anything they said, so I object to her going into that area at all unless the reliability can be established in accordance with the Tadic rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see the necessity of that question. It is not necessary. You are not referring to a particular prisoner or a particular injury which is he is reporting. Even if you were doing that -- will you kindly pass to another question which is not hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, were there occasions when you could hear beatings as they were going on, even if you did not personally see them as they were going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain what happened on those occasions, what it was you could hear, if you know when it was, how often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These instances were frequent. You could see the effects on them, the bruises they had. It was obvious to look at them that they were exposed to torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to what you could see of the injuries on the prisoners, is it the case that sometimes you could hear beatings as they were going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought that was your last question before he gave you the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. I think he gave relevant evidence, but I am not sure it was exactly in response to my question so I am repeating my question because I think it may not have been clear to the witness. Maybe if I can rephrase it it will be more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are asking if he is hearing beatings, even if he did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is exactly right, your Honour. Sir, is it the case that on some occasions you could hear a beating as it was going on, even if you were not yourself able to see it; in other words could you -- let me just ask that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could you tell that there was a beating going on? What kinds of things could you hear that let you know there was a beating going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could hear the cries of the men who were beaten up. You could hear their moans and screams, and that is how I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you just referred to a beating that was recorded on video. First of all, sir, can you tell the court who it was who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps we might have to stop here and come back at 12.00. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness's microphone be turned on? Thank you. Sir, you indicated that there was a particular beating that was recorded on video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the court who recorded it on video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the court who it was who made the tape recording, the video recording? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made the video recording.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the judges exactly what you recorded with your video camera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I recorded the prisoners in the hangar, those who were in the big hangar, in the back, and then I recorded faces of the prisoners and later I heard some cries and screams which were coming from the back of the hangar. Then I went there and I saw that two of the guards whose names were Zijad Landzo and Osman Dedic, that they were beating two prisoners and I recorded that with a camera. I cannot remember exactly the names of the prisoners. On that occasion, they were beating them, and then burnt the socks on the feet of one of them, and then they were burning for about a minute, a minute and a half, then I stopped the recording and I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for a minute. When you say that this occurred in the back of the hangar, do you mean inside the hangar toward the back or do you mean outside the hangar in the back of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The abuse took place in the back of the hangar, the big hangar. It was behind the big hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it inside the hangar or outside the hangar in the back of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was outside the hangar, behind it, behind the back side of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prisoners, can you just tell the judges a little more explicitly what you saw; for instance were the prisoners clothed or not clothed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was completely naked and you could see bruises on his back, and the other one had trousers and socks on, which one of the guards, as I said, later set on fire. That is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw exactly in more detail, what you remember about the beating; for instance, do you know -- can you describe how it was and who it was who set the prisoner's socks on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The socks were set on fire by Zenga. Zenga set the socks on fire on this prisoner, I think he was a taxi driver, as far as I can recall, I cannot remember exactly. I cannot remember who it was who was beating the other prisoner who was completely naked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the prisoner a taxi driver whose name you do not remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember either of the names of the two, the one whose socks were set on fire, he was a taxi driver as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away, sir, were you when you filmed this beating and torture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five to six metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were present, how long were you present filming this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three minutes, because the batteries were running down on the camera and then I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you stop recording? In other words, was the beating finished or did you stop for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the batteries were running flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left was the beating still going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know. I do not know whether it continued or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know approximately when this was? Even if you do not remember a month, or what your duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My duties were also those of a driver. It was some time in summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what happened to this videotape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It stayed behind in Konjic, in the house where I had lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the video is now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you yourself intervene at all to stop what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not intervene because there was nothing I could do, because I was just a guard, same as they were, and my word would not have been of any help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you asked, when you were first interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, were you asked whether or not you had recorded any video or beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were first interviewed by Mr. Milner from the Office of the Prosecutor, were you asked about whether or not you had videotaped any mistreatment of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the truth about that at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess because I was afraid of saying that I had taped it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were at Celebici camp did any prisoners ever die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners died when you were working in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, perhaps 13 or 15. I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how these prisoners died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some died probably due to the beatings, exhaustion, perhaps age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any guards ever tell you anything about their own involvement in the death of any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any prisoners who died while you were working in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of all the prisoners that died -- all the names that you remember of the prisoners who died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Klimenta Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the only name you remember at this time, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I just cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Klimenta, how did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One morning when the prisoners went outside to go to the toilet and for the morning wash, one of the guards was making jokes with him that he was going to kill him and he had a bullet in the barrel. I do not know if he had known about it, he fired the bullet and he hit him, that is how he was killed, at least that was what he said. Whether that was true or not I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear this from the guard who killed the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Samir -- I cannot remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Klimenta have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Keljo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides what you have already -- sir, did you ever see any corpses while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell the judges what you saw about -- exactly what happened when you saw the corpses, how it was that you saw them, what you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wrapped in some blankets, we could not see their bodies, and I was ordered to drive them to the morgue in Konjic and the circumstances of their death, that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, was this on two separate occasions that you saw these corpses, or was there one occasion when you saw two corpses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this at the same time that Keljo was killed, or were these two occasions on different occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that one of the corpses you saw was Keljo's or not? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these two occasions when you were ordered to drive the corpses to the morgue, was this during the time that you were a driver in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did these occasions -- were you ordered to drive these corpses to the morgue because you were a driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who ordered you to bring these corpses to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not 100 per cent certain. I think it was Hazim Delic, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the bodies when you first saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were inside a car, in the back of a car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who loaded the bodies into the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told the names of who these bodies were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the morgue or funeral -- can you tell us where it was that you brought the bodies to, more specifically? For instance, was it a morgue or was it a funeral company? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a funeral company in Konjic, in the town. I cannot remember, I think it was close to the MUP where the cemetery was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the funeral company, did you have to give them any paperwork? Did they ask whose bodies they were? Would you please tell us exactly what happened when you got to the funeral company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not ask for any documents, they simply took them and perhaps they received a telephone call earlier as to what to do with the corpses, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back for a minute to when Keljo -- Mr. Klimenta was killed, do you know, was he killed also during the time that you were a driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a driver most of the time you worked in the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to your two occasions driving bodies to the funeral company, do you know whether or not the funeral company mortuary van also occasionally visited the camp to pick up bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, no, I never saw them. Perhaps they did come when I was not there. Perhaps a vehicle was there, I was not paying any attention to that. Perhaps it was a civilian vehicle that drove them, because many vehicles came and went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were there any investigations into the deaths of any of the prisoners, the 13 to 15 prisoners who died while you worked in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any investigations into the beatings of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to what you have already testified to, did any of, besides what you heard from Mr. Landzo and this person -- I am sorry, what did you say the name of the guard was who told you about what happened to Keljo, Mr. Klimenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not it also could have been Amir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samir, Almir, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, besides what you have talked about or what you heard from Zenga and from Samir or Almir, did you ever hear anyone else who worked in the camp say anything about their own involvement in beating and other mistreatment of prisoners? With respect to mistreatment, I am including sexual assaults.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us from whom you heard this and what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from Hazim Delic, I heard him say that he had already reached number 18, that he had raped 18 Serb women, and he said that he was going to stop once he reached number 100.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were prisoners beaten in Mr. Mucic's presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic know that prisoners were beaten when he was not present?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness has already said no, and I do not know why the distinguished representative of the Prosecution insists. He said he was not there and he said he did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The two questions are not the same. The first one, were prisoners beaten in Mucic's presence; he said no. The second question: whether he knew that they were beaten when he was not there. They are two different questions. I hope you understand that. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did Mr. Mucic know that prisoners were beaten when he was not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He probably knew when he came from town, because he would visit the prison, as he could probably see on them some consequences, bruises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- did you yourself ever speak to Mr. Mucic about the beatings that occurred when he was not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, when we spoke he said that he was doing everything within his powers and he was not able to protect when he was not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you, sir, to mean that you did talk to him about the beatings, and then he gave you this answer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us more specifically what you remember telling Mr. Mucic about the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely what I had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said he cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, even if you cannot remember precisely what you said, do you ever remember discussing with him a specific incident, when you either saw or heard a beating occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion some soldiers came from outside the camp and then they beat one prisoner, and then he shouted a lot, and the next day I told him that these prisoners came from the outside and he said that he could not prevent it. If he had been there perhaps he probably would have prevented it, because there were these other units and other people who were more dangerous to whom one could say nothing. They could simply come to the prison to do whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you told him about this incident, how do you mean by him? Who did you tell about this incident where the prisoner was screaming a lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tell Mr. Mucic from how far away you could hear the screams of this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could hear screaming at quite a distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told Mr. Mucic about how far away you could hear the screams from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also remember talking to Mr. Mucic about the fact that persons who worked in the camp beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you remember; for instance, who did you tell him was mistreating prisoners when he was not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said how Hazim was mistreating the prisoners, and some other guards, like Zenga and the soldiers coming from other parts of Bosnia, from other towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina. When I said that he would say, "well I am doing the best I can". When he was there he would say nobody would touch them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give Mr. Mucic a copy of your videotape of Zenga and Mr. Osman Dedic beating and torturing the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First I was a little scared, and secondly, I thought perhaps they did not know. I do not know why. I thought they would not do anything because I had done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone else besides you ever spoke to Mr. Mucic about the mistreatment of prisoners when he was not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
